The first movement of Rachmaninoff's "Fantasie-Tableaux for 2 Pianos" is in this form. Unusually, the second movement of Bela Bartok's Out of Doors is a chromatic one, and, though simpler, the "June" movement of Tchaikovsky's The Seasons is also a relatively complex example of this genre. Gabriel Faure's ballade is often recorded together with his thirteen pieces in this form, the most famous of which is the third in G flat. Chopin only wrote one for the piano, his F Sharp Minor Op. 60, while the most famous begins "Belle nuit, o nuit amour" and is sung by Giulietta and Nicklausse in Act II of The Tales of Hoffman. Appropriately, one plays as Joseph Porter's boat enters in HMS Pinafore. Name this genre of slow, rolling Venetian boat songs.

Among his few reliefs are his Annunciation for the Cavalcanti Chapel and the putti for his pulpit of the Prato Cathedral. His sought greater expressiveness with his early prophets Jeremiah though he created a very placid St. George for the Or San Michele. His middle period includes an enormous equestrian statue in Padua, while his late work includes a desiccated wooden Mary Magdalene, as well as a stoic Judith Slaying Holofernes, the latter of which stood in the courtyard of the Palazzo Medici opposite another victorious slayer he created who wears only boots and a feathered hat. Name this Renaissance sculptor of the most famous bronze David.

This man inserted a self-portrait in the left side of his imitation of a painting by Dirk van Baburen. His version of the scene shows a red-cloaked man menacingly embracing a smiling women in a yellow shirt and white bonnet, who is holding out her hand to receive a coin. In addition to The Procuress, he also showed himself looking at a woman who stands beside a bed behind a drawn curtain in The Art of Painting. A few dark clouds intrude on the top, and some small figures in black walk on the beach, in his depiction of brick buildings in his river-side home town, View of Delft. Name this artist of The Milk Maid and Girl With a Pearl Earring, a Dutch Baroque figure.

Several of this man's early solo piano works are collected in his Album d'un voyager, and he noted that he could not find a lyrical melody in his second "forgotten waltz." A work characteristic of his Wemar period is a symphonic poem titled Prometheus. Alidor is Lord of the Castle of Love in his sole opera, Don Sanche, and Chasse-Neige and "Will o' the Wisp" are two movements in his difficult set of twelve piano pieces. The composer of a Faust Symphony and some Mephisto Waltzes, he included "Mazeppa" in his collection of Transcendental Etudes. Name this piano virtuoso who used Gypsy melodies of his homeland in the Hungarian Rhapsodies.

This composer's Six Studies for Contralto were written for his Jewish lover, whom he left after his immigration papers did not allow him to accompany her to Berlin. In one of his works, which includes the "banquet scene" overture, Svetozar pledges half his kingdom to a title character. This composer's guitarist friend inspired him to write Jota (HO-tuh) Aragonesa and a later piece called Summer Night in Madrid. In an opera by him, an evil dwarf sorcerer named Chernomor abducts a bride. Another of this man's operas features a hero who leads an invading Polish army astray, Ivan Susanin. Name this composer of A Life for the Tzar and Ruslan and Ludmilla.

One of this man's works shows a giant helmet sitting on top of a castle. In addition to The Capitulation of Sedan, he portrayed a fellow artist on a balloon in NADAR Elevating Photography to Art, and also showed an old man playing against a young man in The Chess Players. He depicts Louis- Phillipe as Gargantua in one of the works in his collection La Caricature, and he also founded the political satire newspaper Le Charivari. He's probably most famous for a work which contains a woman holding a baby sitting next to a man in a top hat and an old woman with a basket on the titular conveyance. Name this French artist of The Third-Class Carriage.

One of this man's overtures was inspired by a Thomas Rowlandson etching and draws upon the rhythm of the Catalan sardana. He adapted the piece Spitfire Prelude and Fugue from the earlier work Duets for Children and wrote a viola concerto premiered by Paul Hindemith. In addition to the film scores for Laurence Olivier's versions of Hamlet and Richard III, he composed the operas The Bear and Trolius and Cressida, but he may be better known for a choral work with text selected by Osbert Sitwell from a Biblical story about a Babylonian king. Name this twentieth-century British composer of the oratorio Belshazzar's Feast.

One painting in the original series by this name shows a man pulling on a turtle next to a water mill, and another shows a tea house after a snowfall. In one painting some boats and a fisherman are shown under the "Thousand Year" bridge, in another a kite can be seen flying above some scaffolding on the left and the tip of a temple located in the "eastern capital" on the right, and in the most famous work in this series two boats can be seen struggling in a great wave, but not a tsunami, off the coast of Kanagawa. Identify this ukiyo-e series of forty-six woodblock prints all depicting the titular mountain from a variety of perspectives by Katsushika Hokusai.

According to its creator, this work was created while "The forest creatures were all sad; the mushrooms did not dance, the elderberries gave no juice for the festival wines," and minor characters in this work include "Dead Bowie" and "Snake Bite." At one point the protagonist compares himself to Gandhi in his hope to be a notable figure, after comparing himself to Bad Horse in front of his crush. "Caring Hands" and "Brand New Day" are from the soundtrack of this work, which also proposes "bashing in minds." name this popular online film, starring Nathan Fillion, Felicia Day, and Neal Patrick Harris, and created by Joss Whedon.

He wrote a ballet in which the Flame enchants all the moths in the room except for the most beautiful, Folia, titled The Lure. He also wrote an opera in which the titular character tells a story to reveal the wife's sexual affairs, titled The Wandering Scholar. That same year he wrote a piece for the BBC Military Band, Hammersmith, and two years earlier he wrote A Moorside Suite, but he is better known for a piece inspired by a vacation in Algeria first entitled Oriental Suite and an opera that is based on an episode from the Mahabharata. Name this British composer of the suite Beni Mora and the opera Savitri, who depicted "the bringer of jollity" and "the bringer of war" in The Planets.

He used a figure in Antonio Pollaiuolo's The Rape of Deianira as the model for Hercules in his Hercules and the Birds of Stymphalis. "The Drummer and Piper" and "Job and His Wife" are the two side panels of this man's Altar of the Three Kings, and portraits by this man include those of Oswolt Krel and the Tucher family. He may be best known for a work that includes an hour glass, an empty balance scale, a polyhedron with a skull on it, and a magic square which gives the date of the work, 1514, in the middle two cells. Also known for woodcuts like his Apocalypse series, name this German engraver of Melancholia I.

His long-time collaboration with drummer Dannie Richmond yielded such politically-charged pieces as "Oh Lord Don't Let Them Drop That Atomic Bomb On Me," and one dedicated to an "All-American heel" from Arkansas which appeared on the same album as his tribute to recently-deceased Lester Young. He teamed up with Max Roach and Duke Ellington to record Money Jungle, and led his own bands in recording such albums as The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady and Pithecanthropus Erectus. Name this man whose songs "Fables of Faubus" and "Goodbye, Pork Pie Hat" featured his virtuosic double bass playing.

He redesigned the church building at St. Luke's Episcopal Church for his friend and biographer Louis Noble, and at his death he left uncompleted a series of paintings titled "The Cross in the World". A mirage-like castle appears in the sky as an angel watches a boy push off in a boat in Youth, the second of four paintings in this man's "Voyage of Life" series. Also known for such works as Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, this man taught Frederic Church and was memorialized in an Asher Durand painting which sees him talking with William Cullen Bryant. Name this painter of the "Course of Empire" series, the founder of the Hudson River School.

This artist depicted the title figure under a tree and raking leaves in his Old Man in Warnemunde, one of several paintings of people in that city that also included Children in the Street and Three Girls at the Beach. A man wearing a bow tie is the only figure in his Self Portrait with a Burning Cigarette, and a Madonna by this artist depicts a nude woman from the torso up, whose arms slowly blend into the background. Better known may be his depiction of a redheaded female Vampyr, or his recollection of his sister Sophie's death in Death in the Sickroom. Name this Norwegian artist who depicted a distorted face on a bridge in The Scream.

This term denotes a Brazilian artistic movement whose greatest literary achievement may be the "Cannibal Manifesto" of Oswald de Andrade. The destruction of a more famous movement of this name may have begun with a poem telling the reader to "Wring the necks of the deceitful swans"; that movement included the authors of such poetry collections as Fiat Lux and The Twilights of the Garden. In addition to Jose Santos Chacono and Leopoldo Lugones, this movement was also associated with the author of Azul. Name this Latin American literary movement founded by Ruben Dario, which gave birth to later movements like ultraismo.

He painted a monastery with a tree on the right side in his circular painting The Charterhouse. He painted a girl in a white dress next to her brother in orange shorts and a black hat in Heneage Lloyd and His Sister, and a less characteristic portrait is that of John Kirby, who is in front of a dark brown background. He shows a man leaning with a long rifle and his wife sitting on a bench in a blue dress next to a plowed field in Robert Andrews and His Wife Frances, though he is better known for a depiction of a young Jonathan Buttall. FTP, name this English portraitist, a rival of Joshua Reynolds who painted The Blue Boy.

Giant eyeball-like objects and scenes of torture abound in this artist's depiction of a gigantic female figure striding through a hellish environment. In addition to Dulle Grit, he painted a scene of a small cross and a crowd of dancers next to a gallows in The Magpie on the Gallows. Another of his paintings shows several breaking wheels being used as skeletons indiscriminately kill, The Triumph of Death. Another one of his paintings shows two men carrying several dishes amid a scene of merriment, The Peasant Wedding. FTP, identify this 17th century Flemish painter famous for scenes such as Hunters in the Snow and Landscape With the Fall of Icarus.

He used Persian myth as the basis for his oratorio Paradise and the Peri and wrote of the love triangle between Siegfried, Golo, and the title woman in his only opera. Two sections of another worked are marked hastig and einfach und zart, those are the middle sections of his ironically titled Humoreske. The sequence "A-E flat – C- B" represents the "Asch" motif in his Carnaval, which also includes sections denoted "Florestan" and "Eusebius". He dedicated Kreisleriana to Chopin, and later works include the five-movement Rhenish Symphony. FTP, identify this husband of Clara Wieck whose first symphony is also known as "Spring".

Bernardo Bellincioni suggested that the title figure of one of his paintings "seemed to listen and not to speak", and the reverse of another of his portraits contains a juniper sprig and a motto translated as "Beauty is Virtue". In addition to Cecilia Gallerani, the titular Lady with an Ermine, and Ginevra de' Benci, he depicted an emaciated figure holding a rock in his outstretched hand in a portrait of St. Jerome. A series of drawings involving a cat being cuddled lend credence to the existence of his Madonna with a Cat; he also painted the Benois Madonna in addition to his most famous Madonna, the Virgin of the Rocks. Name this Italian who drew a Vitruvian Man and painted La Gioconda.

In one painting with this subtitle, Charles Angrand depicts two sailboats on a certain river "at Courbevoie". Three fish appear in the foreground of a Monet painting depicting "Springtime" here, and two people cross a bridge of this name in a Van Gogh painting. However, the most famous depiction of this locale contains a reclining man in a red, sleeveless shirt smoking a pipe, a standing woman in black and violet holding an umbrella, a dog and monkey play- fighting, and some fuzzy trees, all of which are composed of dots of paint. What island in the Seine provided the setting for a Sunday Afternoon painted by Georges Seurat?

One work that Vincenzo Giustiniani commissioned from this artist takes its title from the Eclogues and features Cupid with eagle wings half sitting in the middle of scattered instruments. One depiction of Bacchus, with some peaches on the table and grapes in his left hand, is quite sickly, but in another painting, an attractive, slightly-drunk Bacchus clad in toga holds a goblet of wine. A boy hides cards in his belt and his accomplice peeks a look at the opponent's hand in The Cardsharps. The heightened form of chiaroscuro, tenebrism, was the key feature in The Conversion of St. Paul and The Calling of St. Matthew by what painter?

His "Ray Gun Theatre" artwork was inspired by his meeting with Allan Kaprow in New York City in 1956 where he learned of "happenings", or performative pieces of art. Other works of his include the Crusoe Umbrella in Iowa and Typewriter Eraser at the National Gallery of Art, created after his marriage to Dutch pop artist Coosje van Bruggen, but he is more famous for erecting a sculpture of lipstick resting on a black tank-like base at Yale. FTP, name this Swedish pop sculptor of Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks and Clothespin, noted for giant sculptures of food and classifying his sculptures as "hard" and "soft".

This character writes books in which a girl detective is "supposed to be an orphan, but her old man keeps showing up." She is almost given a record on which a black female, Estelle Fletcher, sings about a little girl whose two front teeth were broken. Besides writing about Hazle Weatherfield, almost getting to listen to "Little Shirley Beans," and watching Robert Bunat's The 39 Steps, she tells her brother that "Daddy's going to kill you" after he got expelled from Pencey Prep, and almost runs away with her brother at the end of the novel she appears in. FTP, who is this younger sister of Holden Caulfield created by J. D. Salinger in Catcher in the Rye?

This artist showed a figure in golden armor flying on a hippogriff stabbing a dragon while the titular maiden is chained to a rock in the sea in his painting Roger Freeing Angelica, while a line of alabaster soldiers made from clouds appear above a figure in a red cape sleeping on his harp in his The Dream of Ossian. In one work Shakespeare, Dante, and Racine surround the title character, who has the personification of the Iliad sitting below him, while another work features a reclining nude that is holding a turquoise curtain on the right and possesses an extra vertebra. FTP, name this artist, who painted The Apotheosis of Homer and Grand Odalisque.

A misplaced pin in this opera leads one character to malign women in the aria, "Aprite un po quegli occhi," while another character expresses his love for Barbarina in the aria, "Voi che sapete." A contract is dissolved when it is revealed that Marcellina is the mother of her betrothed and she decides to marry Bartolo instead, and the page Cherubino is dressed in women's clothes in a scheme to trick Rosina's husband. FTP Count Almaviva realizes the woman he was trying to seduce is not Susanna but his wife at the end of this Mozart opera about the wedding of a barber of Seville.

This composer described Basilio's attempt to save Quiteria from a forced wedding in his opera The Marriage of Camancho. "Die flamme reinight sich vom rauch" is a last section of his cantata depicting a pagan druid sacrifice, The First Walpurgis Night, and he commemorated the four hundredth anniversary of printing in his second symphony. One of his symphonies incorporates a saltarello in the fourth movement, and his third symphony was created after the same trip that inspired the Hebrides Overture. FTP, name this composer of the Italian and Scottish Symphonies, who also wrote the "Wedding March" in his incidental music to A Midsummer Night's Dream.

Upon his graduation from a conservatory, he received no degree in music composition due to failure to complete assignments. Vladimir Horowitz is responsible for the popularity of this man's Tenth Piano sonata, and a special chord featured in symphonies such as Prometheus: Poem of Fire and Poem of Ecstasy was to have been heavily utilized in a work completed by Alexander Nemtin, his unfinished Mysterium. His 24 preludes show him to be an early pioneer of modern dissonance and rhythm. Name this Russian composer best known for the White Mass and Black Mass Sonatas.

This painting sharply contrasts with a similarly named work by Thomas de Keyzer. While this painting depicts an actual event dated to January 16 of the year in which it was painted, most of the figures are believed to have been added later. The title figure is explaining the surprisingly accurate interior of the arm of Aris Kindt, who had been strangled for armed robbery. A man leaning to see casts a shadow on the dead man's face, and a large, open textbook can be seen in the lower right corner, possibly that of Vesalius. FTP name this 1632 painting by Rembrandt depicting a public dissection.
The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp

When painting Washington Crossing the Delaware, Emmanuel Leutze modeled the Delaware River after this river, which was effectively made an international waterway by the 1831 Mannheim Convention. With a length of about 800 miles, it passes through numerous countries, and one national capital. This river's bridge at Arnhem was the site of the failed Operation Market Garden of World War II, which occurred downstream of cities such as Basel, Worms, Speyer, and Rotterdam. Name this major river of Western Europe that starts in the Alps and ends in three distributaries in the Netherlands.

This opera begins with a Passo a Sei, part of a marriage celebration between two unnamed shepherds. In the aria "Asile Hereditaire", one character laments the death of his father Melcthal, that character had earlier sung the aria "Pour notre amour" upon bidding farewell to his beloved, Mathilde. More famous may be the cello solo and flute and English horn duet in its overture, or the aria "Sois Immobile", in which the title character instructs his son Jemmy to stay still before piercing the apple atop his head. What is this last opera by Gioachino Rossini, perhaps best remembered for the "Gallop" section of its overture featured in The Lone Ranger?

The ostinato of the second movement is a faster version of the opening theme in this composer's String Quartet in G Minor. Dante Gabriel Rosetti's "The Blessed Damozel" forms the basis for his La Damoiselle Elue. The solo instrument imitates a guitar through pizzicato in the second movement of his Sonata for Cello and Piano, which was dedicated to his daughter Claude-Emma, to whom he also dedicated the ballet The Box of Toys and the song cycle Children's Corner. Best known for a passage in his Suite bergamesque, name this French composer of La Mer and "Claire de Lune".

Although the faces of the subjects are hidden the artist described the one on the right as an old man of seventy years, and the one on the left as a young fellow in his filthy tattered shirt. The young man is lifting a large boulder and the old one is down on one knee poised to strike with a long hammer. The painting was housed in Dresden during World War II and may have been destroyed. FTP name this oil painting by Gustave Courbet of two guys cracking rocks.

A sequel to this opera, entitled Polly, debuted one year later. Lincoln's Inn Fields was the site for its 1728 premiere; the opera itself lampooned Robert Walpole's Whig administration, with characters such as the loquatious Mrs. Trapes, the fence Jeremy Peachum and the infamous highwayman Captain Macheath. What opera was scored by John Pepusch and written by John Gay, and was the inspiration for Kurt Weill's (VILES) Threepenny Opera?

He gave the funeral oration for the artist Thomas Cole, with whom he is depicted in the painting Kindred Spirits by Asher B. Durand. During his later life he was preoccupied with his blank verse translation of the Iliad, which he published in 1870, in his ongoing role as part owner and editor-in-chief of the New York Evening Post. His most famous poem, published when he was only 17, tells of "The innumerable caravan which moves / To that mysterious realm, where each shall take / His chamber in the silent halls of death." name this man best known for poems such as "The Death of the Flowers" and "Thanatopsis."

Regarded as a landscape specialist during his youth, it is known that he painted part of the background of another artist's portait at least once. His favorite pieces were his landscapes, such as Sunset: Carthorses drinking at a Stream, but another genre brought him fame. He became known for portraits such as Mr. And Mrs. Robert Andrews, and his most famous work, depicting Jonathan Buttall, was sfamous for the striking contrast in the color of the background and the subject's clothes. FTP, name this English portraitist most famous for his Blue Boy.

What was originally supposed to be this work's final movement was instead placed in its composer's A minor string quartet. Its first movement, marked un poco maestoso, opens with the horns playing pianissimo triplets dropping from D to A, then down to D again, followed by a fortissimo establishing the tonic key of D minor. The scherzo and trio are moved up to the second movement, and themes from all three prior movements are reprised in the fourth movement before the lower strings take up its most familiar theme. Variations on that same theme are incorporated as a Turkish march, orchestral fugue, and finally a vocal quartet whose voices climb towards the Elysium mentioned in the libretto. FTP name this symphony which features the words of Schiller put to music as 'Ode to Joy'.

In its second act, Bobby, pretending to be Bela Zangler, sings a duet of "What Causes That" with the real Bela, each of them lamenting their unrequited love for different women. Premiering on Broadway in 1992, its plot was adapted from the 1930's Girl Crazy. Bobby Child, a New York banker, must go to Deadrock Nevada to foreclose on a theater, but he falls in love with Polly, the daughter of the theater owner, and convinces her to put together a show to save the theater. The townsfolk have all got rhythm, but more mayhem ensues before the inevitable happy ending. FTP, name this musical written around the songs of George and Ira Gershwin.

Some of his later work included portraits of Edith Mahon and his own wife, and his own self-portrait shows himself with a resigned face, in a warm light, dressed in a coat and tie. Unlike other American portraitists, he refused to flatter his clients in order to gain financial compensation, and for this he received meager funds in his lifetime. His most famous painting was sold for two hundred dollars to its namesake institution, after critics deemed as "unsightly" a bloodied hand of a surgeon. FTP, name this Pennsylvania born artist, most famous for "The Gross Clinic."

Serge has just spent 200,000 francs on a painting which, to Marc's disgust, is nothing but white lines on a white background. Serge defends his purchase, and Marc brings in Yvan to take his side, but Yvan waffles, wanting to please them both. In the end, Serge magnaminously allows Marc to draw on the painting with a felt tip marker, knowing the ink will be easily removable. As they wash away the little skier that Marc drew, Marc declares that the painting "represents a man who moves across a space, and disappears." FTP, name this play by Yasmina Reza.

Pictures of the Sibyls of Eritrea and Cumae next to Micah and Zechariah, and the donors Elisabeth Borluut and Joos (YOOS) Vijd (VIDE) adorn some of the outside panels of this polyptych in St. Bavo's Cathedral. A rhymed quatrain on the frame confirms that it was begun by Hubert. The dome of Utrecht was added in the background of the central panel, which includes the Fountain of Life in the Adoration of the Lamb. FTP name this huge altarpiece primarily attributed to Jan van Eyck.

In 1854 he traveled to Palestine to get an authentic setting for religious paintings such as The Scapegoat and The Finding of Christ in the Temple. Other religious works include The Light of the World. He took many subjects from literature, such as Isabella and the Pot of Basil and The Lady of Shallot. For 10 points--name this English painter who founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood with Dante Gabriel Rosetti and John Everett Millais.

In 1929, he succeeded Arturo Toscanini as musical director of La Scala in Milan, and wrote the opera Nerone, which glorified Mussolini. While he tried to revive the commedia in La maschere, he is better known as an exponent of the verismo style of opera. His best-known work, featuring characters such as Alfio, village girls Lola and Santuzza, and the soldier Turiddu, is based on a Sicilian melodrama by Giovanni Verga. For 10 points--name this composer of Cavalleria Rusticana.

He was noted for his sculptures of animals such as A Cow in the Marketplace of Athens though neither that nor any other of his works depicting animals have survived. Thought to have been a pupil of Ageladas of Argos, and a native of Eleutherae, he nevertheless worked mainly in Athens, and produced such statues as Ladas the Runner. Sculpting mainly in bronze, his Athena and Marysas survives as a Roman copy. FTP, name this classical Greek sculptor noted for his sculptures of athletes in motion such as Discobolus.

In Fall 2003 the Prado exhibited eight of his tapestries depicting the Life of Achilles. Engaged as a diplomat earlier in his career, it was in this capacity in England, a stay in which he completed nine canvases for the ceiling of the Banqueting Palace at Whitehall. Following his first marriage in 1609, he completed a Double Portrait in a Honeysuckle Bower, but two works completed in following 4 years, the Raising of and Descent from the Cross, would outdo that piece. FTP name this Flemish baroque painter who influenced Rembrandt, best known for his use of plump women as subject matter.

Violinist Eduard Remenyi falsely claimed he composed them, though their composer claimed originality for only three of this collection's twenty-one pieces. Originally written for two pianos, they were set for violin and piano by Joseph Joachim and Dvorak orchestrated the last four. Begun when the composer worked in Detmold, they were published in two sets in 1869 and 1880 and were based in Gypsy tunes. FTP, identify this Brahms collection, a set of dances named for the home nation of the Magyar.

Set in the early seventeenth century, this opera's title character spends most of the opera hiding in a monastery. The man who spurs the action is Sobinin, who cannot marry his beloved Antoninda until her father is certain that a true tsar sits on the throne. The plot twists in the second act when it is revealed that a group of Poles are plotting to make a Pole tsar by capturing the chosen Russian tsar. Antoninda's father, Ivan Susanin, sacrifices himself to foil the Polish plot in, FTP, what 1836 opera by Glinka?

During the Reign of Terror, he was saved from execution by the efforts of his admirer David, but he was unable to adjust to the new styles of painting, and died in poverty. A master of the "fa presto" technique, he flourished under the patronage of Madame de Pompadour and Madame de Barry, who decorated their apartments with his sentimental murals. FTP, name this rococo painter of "The Crowning of Love," "The Love Letter," and "The Swing."

The fourteenth-century version consists of eleven-syllable lines, arranged as two or three tercets, followed by a couplet, with different music, known as the ritornello. The sixteenth- century version is much freer, with three to fourteen lines of seven or eleven syllables each. FTP, Francesco Landini, Costanzo Festa, Thomas Morley, and Claudio Monteverdi all excelled at what form of secular choral music?

The caption on the outside reads, "He must increase, and I must decrease," and is printed next to John the Baptist, who stands to the left of a traditional crucifixion scene. The inside depicts the Annunciation, the Angel Concert for Madonna and Child, and the brightly-colored Resurrection, which seems to anticipate the style of William Blake. FTP, name this artwork painted for the monastery of St. Anthony by Matthias Gruenwald.

Oscar-nominated composer Mark Isham, CNN legal analyst Greta Van Susteren, jazz great Chick Corea, Jenna Elfman of _Dharma & Greg_, Priscilla and Lisa Marie Presley, and Kirstie Alley are all members. Anne Archer has been spoken out against restrictive German laws against it, as has John Travolta, who joined the year before he joined the cast of _Welcome Back Kotter_. FTP, name this celebrity-friendly "religion," the brainchild of L. Ron Hubbard.

Pts: Although his younger brother called him "the greatest painter in creation," some scholars doubt whether he actually existed. Works attributed to him include "Three Marys at the Tomb" and the Turin-Milan Book of Hours. 5 pts: He began work on the Ghent Altarpiece, which was completed after his death by his younger brother Jan.

Pts: Richard Strauss called this Russian 'mein Don Quixote' and wrote many solo lines in his compositions especially for him. He became a professor at the University of Southern California, has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and sponsored two world-class chess tournaments in the 1960's.

The Vaughan-type painting of his most famous subject shows a head and torso, while the Landsdowne type is a full-body portrait. The Athenaeum type is very frequently reproduced even though the bottom third of his canvas was left blank. FTP, name this artist best known for his three portraits of George Washington.

When Chretien de Troyes (twah) left this work unfinished at his death, Wolfram von Eschenbach rewrote and completed it in German. Along the way, Eschenbach changed the title character's quest object to a stone tray which supplied the bearer with all manner of meats and alcohol. FTP, name this tale about an Arthurian knight in pursuit of the Holy Grail, which Richard Wagner later adapted for opera.

Cave paintings show that these animals, called Oomingmak or "Bearded One" by the Inuit, lived as far south as Spain during the Pleistocene. Surviving in the Arctic, they were exterminated in Alaska and nearly wiped out in Canada in part because their defensive herd circles make them easy rifle targets. FTP, what are these smelly mammals more closely related to sheep and goats than cattle, despite what their common name suggests?

Originating in Oaxaca and Jalisco provinces, it was made famous by artists like Cirilo Marmolejo early in this century. Featuring violins, guitarron, guitar, trumpets, and percussion instruments like the marimba, its name may derive from the French word for "marriage." FTP, what Mexican style became so popular that its name became a slang term for any musician, including the title character of a 1992 Robert Rodriguez film?

He painted the features of the human face without drawing lines, relying on the use of color changes alone. His arrangements often show the main subject separated from the viewer by some object, such as the drapery in _The Letter_ and the table in _The Kitchen Maid_. FTP, name this painter of _Woman Holding a Balance_ and _View of Delft_ whose approximately thirty surviving works are among the rarest in all of art.

He received training from a portrait painter named Stein and spent two years at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts before painting landscapes that earned him the patronage of John Trumbull. His works include landscapes like _The Ox-Bow_, classically-themed works like _The Architects Dream_, and religious works like _The Expulsion of Adam and Eve from the Garden of Eden_. FTP, name this painter and leading figure of the Hudson River School.

Strife among noblemen, the alliance between Guillaume d'Orange and Louis the Pious, and struggles against the Moors were popular subjects of these epics, while common themes included chivalry and courtly love. They survive in manuscripts dating from the 11th to 15th centuries, and each of the near eighty in existence is thousands of lines long. FTP, name these medieval French "songs of great deeds," the most famous of which is the _Song of Roland_.

Characters include a mediocre opera company which is sold into slavery by its disgruntled impresario; the pedantic tutor who is eaten by a group of starving castaways; and Catherine the Great, who becomes the lover of the title character. It also features a mysterious ghost, but in this version of the story, the ghost does not kill the hero, since it is really a woman in disguise who is trying to seduce him. FTP, name this satirical epic by Lord Byron.

The first composer hired to write it was Tcherepnin, who completed two scenes before he quarreled with his choreographer and quit. His replacement, Liadov, was fired for procrastination. The job was then offered to Glazunov, who declined it, as did Sokolov. In desperation, impresario Serge Diaghilev turned to an unknown 27-year-old, and the rest is history. FTP, name this 1911 ballet inspired by Russian folklore and written by Igor Stravinsky.

No other composer's genius ever flared up as suddenly, or collapsed as rapidly, as that of this man. In 1887, at the age of 27 and with no significant works to his name, he began setting the poems of Eduard Moricke to music and produced 174 songs, most of which are minor masterpieces. At 29, he began to go insane, and never wrote anything of note again. FTP, name this hard-luck Austrian, the greatest composer of Lieder after Schumann.

His early works, such as the Fagus Shoe Factory, are characterized by walls of glass with barely-visible support structures. His last project, the Cambridge Architects' Co-Op,reflected his belief in anonymous group design. His most important project at tempted to unify architecture, engineering, and visual art, and brought together such luminaries as Mies van der Rohe, Klee, and Kandinsky. FTP, name this founder of the Bauhaus.

In a Carl Spitteler work he is ``Long-Suffering'', while a Jacques Lipchitz statue has him ``Strangling the Vulture''. Pedro Calderon de la Barca wrote of his ``Statue'' while Schubert and Beethoven each used him as a subject. Gide wrote of him ``Misbound'', in homage to works of Percy Shelly and Aeschylus. Name this figure of Greek myth to whom Mary Shelley refers in her subtitle of ``Frankenstein''.

It was the Yellow Book movement in England and the Jugendstil (YOO-gunt- shteel) movement in Germany. Characterized by elaborate use of flowery and ornamental designs, its leading figures include poster artist Teophile Steinlen, subway designer Hector Guimard, and stage designer Leon Bakst. FTP, name this turn-of-the-century art movement also associated with Antonio Gaudi, Aubrey Beardsley, and Louis Tiffany.

This painting was inspired by a Pierre Corneille tragedy, although the scene that it depicts did not appear in the actual play. The title characters, two of whom will not return home alive, stand at far left, their right arms extended towards their father, who holds three swords in the air. FTP, name this painting about three brothers about to fight a duel with the Curiatii, an early masterpiece of Jacques-Louis David.

The term comes from the Greek for "sing," and the first ones were probably written as choral pieces in Greek drama. The oldest surviving ones were written by Alcman. Andrew Marvell's is written in the Horatian manner "upon Cromwell's Return from London." Pindaric ones have been written by Ben Jonson, John Milton, and Thomas Gray. FTP, identify this type of ceremonious poem also associated with John Keats.

This artist used classical ruins to symbolize the temporary nature of material things, such as in his Marriage of St. Giustina, and his frescoes at the Villa Barbaro include portraits of the Barbaro family and pets in rooms like the Hall of Olympus and the Room of the Little Dog. In Supper at Emmaus he introduced several superfluous characters, including two children playing with a dog, into a traditional religious scene. This artist's placement of nontheological figures in religious scenes later got him in trouble with the Inquisition when he added soldiers, dwarves, animals and revelers to a depiction of the Last Supper. Who was this painter of The Marriage at Cana and Feast in the House of Levi?

One of this type of composition was written when the daughter of the composer's friend died suddenly of polio, and Samuel Barber's was rejected by its commissioner after Barber presented the perpetuum mobile third movement. Leopold Auer refused to premiere one of these in D major, saying it was unplayable, a term also applied to another one in D major whose final cadenza is accompanied by orchestra. A famous example in e minor is notable for its pioneering omission of an orchestral introduction and was written by Mendelssohn, and Vivaldi wrote a ubiquitous collection of these titled The Four Seasons. Name this type of solo composition for a certain stringed instrument.

Composer Henri Lazarof wrote a string octet inspired by a visit to this location, which gained a new rotunda in the early 1800s. It contains the Nahuatl Florentine Codex and the Erinna papyrus. This location is known for unusual columns that are wider at the top than at the bottom, and possibly its most famous feature is a pietra serena sandstone staircase with oval stairs that leads into the main reading room. Name, this Mannerist construction, designed by Michelangelo to house Pope Clement VII's books.

The uppermost image in this painting is the cross which adorns the church at the top. A small red hat adorns the green man on the right of this canvas. The grape-bunch-like tree in the central-bottom part of the painting is a symbol of life, and the farmer and cow looking at each other in the foreground represent the give and take of agricultural life. In the distance, a man with a hoe walks along a road along with an upside down woman fiddling. Name, this 1911 work combining French surrealist technique with Yiddish folk themes by Marc Chagall.

This composer depicted a "Firemen's Parade on Main Street" in "Gong on the Hook and Ladder", and his early works include "Song for the Harvest Season". He set Vachel Lindsay's poem "General William Booth Enters into Heaven" to music, and "Children's Day Parade" and "Old Folks Gatherin" are movements in his third symphony, which contains many church hymns, The Camp Meeting. His second symphony contains a "Bronx cheer ending", written as a screw you to his teacher Horatio Parker, while another of his works represents strings as the silence of the Druids and a trumpet repeatedly asking the title entity. Name this composer of "Central Park in the Dark" "The Unanswered Question" who included "The Housatonic at Stockbridge" and two other movements in his Three Places in New England.

The fourth of these compositions does not make clear whether tubular bells or a glockenspiel is required for its finale, and was nick named Barkbrod by one critic due to its bleakness. The finale of the fifth features a melody modeled on a swan call, and like the third is in three movements, while an ascending c major scale opens the seventh, which is written entirely in that key and C minor in only one movement. The composer burned his sketches for an eighth of these, although his tone poem Tapiola is often considered as an eighth. Identify these compositions, the second of which has a climaxing finale often associated with Finnish nationalism.

This artist is noted for his photograms, which he renamed after himself. Many of his works are assemblages such as Object to be Destroyed which is a metronome with a picture of an eye on its pendulum. He is also known for his photographs, including Tears and Le Violon d'Ingres, a photograph of the back of a nude woman that he then drew on to resemble a violin. Name this artist, known for his Gift of an iron with nails on it.

This painter of the Vision of the Blessed Herman Joseph also depicted two cherubs playing in the top right even as an aquatic nymph holds out a piece of paper in his Rinaldo and Armida, while another painting depicts a monkey resting on the arm of the dwarf Jeffrey Hudson, who stands next to Henrietta Maria. Religious works of his include Christ with St. Dominic and The Vision of St. Augustine, while other famous subjects of his portraits include Cardinal Bentivoglio and Philip, Lord Wharton. Once hired by Thomas Howard at the court of the Earl of Arundel, one of his paintings depicts his subject three times over while another depicts that subject in a silver doublet. That patron, Charles I, was this man's primary benefactor. Name this former student of Rubens.

In this work, fairies are demanded to dance in the aria "Sul fil d'un soffio etesio" whiel two characters are chastised in "Che dunque l'onore? Una parola!" The protagonist asks "È sogno o realtà?" and this work ends with the title character singing the fugue "Tutto nel mondo è burla... Tutti gabbati!" The title character of this work is disguised as the Black Huntsman and spends some time in a dirty laundry basket. Doctor Caius captures Bardolph and Fenton marries Nannetta at the end of this work, and this work sees Mistress Quickly announce the coming of Ford. Name this work about a certain fat knight, a Verdi opera adapted from The Merry Wives of Windsor.

The three works which first brought him attention were a symphony in C major, an overture to the Corneille play Polyeucte, and the cantata Velleda. From 1912 until his 1935 death, this man published only two original works, the Sonnet de Ronsard and a piano tribute on the death of Claude Debussy consisting on variations from Afternoon of a Faun. He used a whole-tone scale in his opera Ariane and Bluebeard, and Goethe's poem "Zauberlehrling" inspired his most noted piece, a tone poem about a mischievous magical novice. Name this composer of The Sorcerer's Apprentice.

This man created the altar panels showing the Passion of Christ and the martyrdom of St. Sebastian in the Church of St. Florian at Linz. His 1510 St. George and the Dragon devotes most of its attention to a forest, presaging his role, along with Lucas Cranach the Elder, as one of the leading members of the Danube School. His Regensburg Landscapes became the first nature paintings without human figures created in 1500 years. In another painting by this creator of Landscape With a Footbridge, rays of light emerge from a vortex at the right and lavishly rendered clouds, islands, mountains, and lakes fill the top of the canvas, behind a sign with five lines of text on it and above two enormous armies. Name this painter of The Battle of Alexander at Issus.

His professional music career began as part of Michael Pamer's orchestra, where he played the viola. His work at the Sperl garnered him the nickname "the Austrian Napoleon." The inspiration for his major work was a man who worked as Schwarzenberg's chief of staff and led the victories at Custoza and Novara before becomming governor of Lombardy-Venetia throughout the 1850s. Name this man, the composer of the "Radetzky March" and the father of the similarly-named "Waltz King."

The works Maggy and Horse were created by the leading sculptor of this movement, Raymond Duchamp-Villon. One association of painters working in this style called itself the Section d'Or. Robert Delaunay's aggressive colors transformed it into Orphism, and another exponent of this movement invented papier collé and painted Houses at L'Estaque. The painter of The Breakfast Table, Juan Gris, long used its synthetic form, which developed from its earlier analytic phase. Name this movement led by Georges Braque and Pablo Picasso, which showed multiple sides of objects simultaneously and embraced geometric figures.

An important document of this artist's creative process is his red chalk and silverpoint sketch before a portrait of Jacob Meyer and his wife. His Passion Scenes are found in the Basel Town Hall, and this creator of the Solothum Altarpiece also did a woodcut series about the Dance of Death. Texts he illustrated include the German Bible translation made by Martin Luther and In Praise of Folly, and this painter of Madonna of Burgomaster Meyer also painted portraits of such figures as Thomas More and Henry VIII. In another of his works, a bird, a frustrum, a lute, two globes, and an elongated skull adorn the room where the titular diplomats stand. Name this painter of The French Ambassadors.

This man joined Herbert Read, Paul Nash, Ben Nicholson, and another longtime colleague in the artistic circle Unit One. His first public commission was the North Wind project undertaken by the London Transport Board, while the Northampton Church of St. Matthew hosts his Madonna and Child. The Warrior With Shield series was one of the few male subjects he created after experiencing an epiphany at the Trocadero Museum, where he viewed a Chac Mool and decided to create a female equivalent. His career path often intersected with that of Barbara Hepworth, the other major figure, besides this man, in twentieth-century English sculpture. Name this creator of many Reclining Figures.

He enjoyed his first great success in 1822 for his opera Zoraida di Granata. He drew from a Schiller play for his 1835 opera Maria Stuarda, and he wrote a Larghetto for Piano in A minor based on the aria Una furtiva lagrima; that aria is sung by Nemorino in Act II of his opera The Elixir of Love. Drawing heavily from Sir Walter Scott, both Il Castello di Kenilworth and a work concerning the tragic love of Edgardo and the title character are operas by, which Italian composer of Lucia di Lammermoor?

A black dog is laying at the far right of this painting, while a strange white bird at the far left, in the artist's words, "represents the uselessness of words." In the upper right-hand corner of the painting is the artist's signature and the date of the painting's creation, 1897, while in the upper left-hand corner is the painting's title, inspired by a particular catechism during the artist's time in a seminary near Orléans. Depicting a blue Buddha and a progression of aging Tahitian women symbolizing the cycle of life, this is, what inquisitve masterpiece of Paul Gauguin?
Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?

The composer named his villa after this composition. The title objects can be found in four sites at different times of day, the first of which shows the influence of Debussy. That section is set with children plaing inthe Villa Borghese in the daytime; the others are in the Catacombs, the Appian Way, and the Janiculum at night. That section includes the recorded song of a nightingale. Name this second part of a trilogy about the capital of Italy by Ottorini Resphighi.

The first three works in his most famous series were displayed as "degenerate art" and destroyed by the Nazis. His "Yellow-Red-Blue" was a product with his association with Walter Gropius and the Bauhaus, where he taught drawing classes. Together with his friend Franz Mark he founded a group which came to be known by the title of one of his paintings. Name this Russian author of "Concerning the Spiritual in Art" and "Point and Line to Plane," painter of the Composition series and "Der Blaue Reiter," one of the first modern abstract painters.

She worked as a teacher at Longfellow Elementary School until 1969 after which she taught at the John F. Kennedy Elementary School. She proceeded to earn a Master of Library Science degree, and worked at the Houston Public Library and as a librarian at Dawson Elementary School until 1977, when she met her future husband at the home of a mutual friend. FTP, what First Lady has championed education and reading issues as the wife of the 43rd President of the United States?

Beginning as a court entertainment, around 1610 its simple parts were extended and joined together to form scenes, called divertissements, which culminated in its later form. In 1661, Louis XIV founded an academy for it, and in 1708, it moved out of the royal courts and into public performance halls. Italian influence added elevation to the movements, and its costumes were advanced by Marie Camargo and Marie Sallé. FTP, name this art form whose modern proponents include Nijinsky and Balanchine.

This man's androgyny served as the title of a burlesque opera by Francis Polenc and his honest commentary on sexual pleasure resulted in his blinding. Among his prophecies were a warning to Pentheus to recognize and honor Dionysus when he first appeared in Thebes, a prediction of the greatness of Hercules, and advice to Odysseus on how to placate Poseidon. FTP, who was this famous prophet of Thebes that revealed to Oedipus how he had unknowingly murdered his own father?

This book has drawn comparisons to The Grapes of Wrath and was similarly adapted for stage and film. Set in the remote village of Ndotsheni in the Natal Province of Eastern South Africa in 1948, the book revolves around a minister who has seen his immediate family fragment, and departs to the city of Johannesburg. Reverend Stephen Kumalo tries to adhere to the old ways, but the emerging South Africa has brought about the destruction of the tribal communities. FTP name this South African book by Alan Paton.

Although he died in 1957, he did not compose any music during the last 28 years of his life. He did not like the piano and considered it "unsatisfactory" and "ungrateful". The creator of seven symphonies – and, indeed, he was considered his country's greatest symphonist – he is better known for his tone poems, including Valse Triste. FTP, name this composer of a work banned by czarist Russia, 1899's Finlandia.

Blind Harry composed a descriptive though inaccurate account of him, claiming he fought for Philip the Fair against the English in Gascony. His first exploit of note was the murder of Thomas Hazelrigg, the Sheriff of Lanarak. He spent seven years, from 1298 until his betrayal and execution in 1305, conducting a guerilla campaign after his defeat by Edward I at Falkirk. FTP name this victor of Stirling Bridge, the Scottish patriot portrayed by Mel Gibson in the film Braveheart.

Among this artist's favorite subjects was death, which he sometimes eroticized, as in Death and the Maiden. The death of his own sister, as depicted in Death in the Sickroom, is entirely solemn even though it is rendered in the expressionist style this artist pioneered. His most famous work is rendered in the same style, though its subject is decidedly different: a man standing on a bridge, his whole body twisted in a cry of existential anguish. FTP, name this painter of The Scream.

For a Euclidean plane the length of routes composed of orthogonal segments is given by the taxicab one of these. A non-negative function of two arguments, it obeys the triangle inequality, is symmetric, and evaluates to zero when its arguments are identical. Simply stated, this function describes the distance between neighboring points within a given set. FTP, what is this word, which also is the common name for the SI system of measurement?

Taking place about fifty miles southwest of its namesake, Satchidananda opened it by proclaiming that music is "the celestial sound that controls the whole universe." Its first act was Sweetwater and it was attended by over 400,000 people who camped on a Bethel dairy farm owned by Max Yasgur. Featuring such headliners as The Who, Jimi Hendrix, and the Grateful Dead, FTP, what was this 1969 festival in upstate New York billed as "three days of peace, love, and music"?

Derived from the text of Joel 2:31 as found in the Vulgate, it is commonly played on All Souls Day. Composed by a disciple of Francis of Assisi, Thomas de Celano, in the 13th century, it is found in Liszt's Todtentanz, Rachmaninoff's Variations on a Theme of Paganini, and Isle of the Dead. FTP, name this piece, featured in the 5th movement of Berlioz Symphony Fantastique, as well as in the Requiem Mass, whose name means "Day of Wrath"

Long attributed to Pieter de Hooch, this work was purchased by Hitler in 1940 and stored in a salt mine near Vienna during World War II. The woman at center right, with her blue dress, trumpet, and crown of laurels, is generally understood to be the muse Clio, as described in Cesare Ripa's Iconologia, while the painter himself, having just completed painting the blue laurels, is shown in a black beret at his easel. FTP, name the painting that is generally considered the greatest work of Jan Vermeer.

Scholars still disagree whether or not this man or Josep Maria Jujol created perhaps the most famous park benches in the world. They sit atop The Chamber of a Hundred Columns in Park Güell, also designed by this man. Its most striking features are perhaps the undulating design and pottery shards creating a colorful mosaic, defining features in this architect's work. FTP, name this man who designed hundreds of casas in Barcelona as well as the unfinished La Sagrada Familia.

This New Jersey artist was born in 1796 and earned a living at the Bureau of Printing and Engraving. This landscape artist featured Catskill, Adirondack, and White Mountain scenes in such paintings as Early Morning at Cold Spring. FTP, who is this member of the Hudson River School who featured his friends William Cullen Bryant and Thomas Cole in his Kindred Spirits?

Based on La Dame aux camélias by the younger Alexandre Dumas, it opens with at a Paris party thrown by the title figure who meets a man with whom she begins a relationship. Several months later, the man's father Giorgio Germont forces the couple to separate and when they encounter each other at Flora's party, they fight. Act Three finds Alfredo attempting to reconcile with Violetta Valery, who is dying of consumption. FTP, what is this opera about a courtesan by Giuseppe Verdi?
